passage: I'm Tenzin, and last month I tried something new. Raghav and I were on the hostel roof after exams, and he asked how things were at home since my parents separated. Normally I'd say "fine" and find a reason to leave. I felt that exact pull, my hand already on my phone. This time I said, "I want to leave right now. That's what I do when people ask." Raghav just nodded and waited. So I stayed. I told him one small thing: that I hadn't gone home at Diwali because the house feels too quiet now. That was all. He said, "Thanks for telling me," and passed me the chips. Nothing bad happened. The next week I told him a little more.

qa.q: Where were Tenzin and Raghav when Raghav asked about home?
qa.a: They were on the hostel roof after exams.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Raghav asked about home, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tenzin felt the urge to escape; Tenzin's hand was already on the phone, ready to find a reason to leave.

qa.q: What turning point came on the roof, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Tenzin said the urge to leave out loud and stayed to share one small thing, and when nothing bad happened, sharing more became easier.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Tenzin admitted wanting to leave?
qa.a: He may have felt trusted, and it helped him know to wait quietly instead of pushing.

grounding: A student notices the pull to withdraw, names it aloud, stays and shares one small truth with a safe friend, and finds it is met kindly.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Hansa, design studio internship.
Tushar, 21, usually goes silent in feedback meetings and leaves for "a call". Today, when the team asked what he found hard about the brief, he started gathering his sketches, then stopped. "I'm noticing I want to walk out," he said. "Give me a second." He stayed. He told us he'd been stuck for three days and hadn't asked because he hates needing help. Nobody made a fuss; Farida offered to pair with him. He stayed ten minutes past the meeting, sketching with her.
Next step: a quiet check-in with him on Friday, low-key, to keep the door open.

qa.q: How long had Tushar been stuck on the brief?
qa.a: He had been stuck for three days.

qa.q: Why had Tushar not asked for help before?
qa.a: He hates needing help, perhaps fearing it would make him look weak or bring a bad reaction.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar make when he wanted to walk out, and what came of it?
qa.a: He named the urge aloud, asked for a second and stayed to admit he was stuck, which led to Farida offering to pair with him.

qa.q: How might the team see Tushar after this meeting?
qa.a: They may find him more approachable, someone who will now say when he is stuck.

grounding: A supervisor notes an intern who names his urge to withdraw, stays past his comfort and shares a small need with a safe team.

passage:
Monday: After their fight about his job move, Nitin went silent. Jahnavi followed him from the kitchen to the balcony. "Talk to me! Why do you always do this?" He put on his headphones and went for a walk. She sent nine messages. No reply till midnight.
Thursday: At the next disagreement, she tried something different. "I can see you're shutting down. I need us to finish this. Can we pick it up on Sunday evening, after dinner?" He blinked, then nodded.
Sunday: At eight he came to the table, a bit stiff, and talked for twenty minutes. When he began drifting off again, Jahnavi said calmly, "It's okay to pause. It's not okay to vanish for days. That's my limit." He sat back down.

qa.q: How many messages did Jahnavi send on Monday?
qa.a: She sent nine messages.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on Monday when she followed Nitin, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt shut out and desperate; she followed him from room to room and asked why he always does this.

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it work better?
qa.a: She calmly named his shutting down and asked to continue at a set time, which gave him space without dropping her need.

qa.q: How might Nitin experience a calm request compared with being chased?
qa.a: Being chased probably made him feel cornered, so he left; a calm, timed request felt manageable, so he came back.

grounding: Over a week, a woman whose partner goes quiet in conflict moves from chasing him to calm, direct requests and a clear personal limit.

passage: Come, sit with your old Sarita ammachi. When I married your grandfather Thomas, I was twenty-five and he was a closed box. Any quarrel, he would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours. I used to run after him, crying, pulling his sleeve, and he only went further, to the fish market, anywhere. One evening my own mother said, "You are chasing a cat. Sit still and tell him plainly." So the next time, I said, "Thomas, when you leave in the middle, I feel alone. Come back in one hour and we'll finish." Then I made my tea and did not follow. He came back in forty minutes. It took years, but he learned to stay. And I learned to stop running.

qa.q: Where would Thomas go after a quarrel?
qa.a: He would walk out to the church compound and sit there for hours.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel when Thomas left in the middle of a quarrel?
qa.a: She felt alone and upset, which is why she used to run after him crying.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Sarita handled quarrels?
qa.a: She told Thomas plainly how she felt, asked him to come back in one hour and stopped following him.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when Sarita stopped chasing him?
qa.a: He probably felt less cornered, which made it easier to return on his own; he came back in forty minutes.

grounding: A grandmother recalls feeling shut out by a husband who left during quarrels, and how calm, plain requests worked better than chasing.

passage: In their small Lima apartment, Camila, two, toddles toward her mother with a picture book. A door slams downstairs. Rosa gasps and flinches, eyes wide. Camila stops halfway, freezes, then backs toward the sofa, staring at her mother's face. Rosa breathes, kneels and softens her voice: "Just a door, mi amor." Camila edges closer, then stops again. Tomorrow Rosa will tell the clinic nurse how jumpy she has been since the break-in.

qa.q: What was Camila carrying toward her mother?
qa.a: She was carrying a picture book.

qa.q: What might Camila be feeling when she freezes halfway and stares at Rosa's face?
qa.a: She seems scared and confused, because her mother, who usually comforts her, suddenly looks frightened.

qa.q: What step is Rosa planning, and why might it help Camila too?
qa.a: She plans to tell the clinic nurse how jumpy she has been; getting support for her own fear can help her be a calmer, safer base for Camila.

qa.q: What is it like for Rosa when Camila backs away from her?
qa.a: It is probably painful and worrying, and she softens her voice to win back Camila's trust.

grounding: A toddler moves toward her mother, then freezes and backs away because her comforting mother is herself frightened.

passage: I'm Nirmala, the helper at the colony crèche. When Ujjwal's mother comes at five, he runs toward her, then stops a step away and turns to the wall. Sometimes he walks to her backwards. She looks scared herself, eyes red, jumping when anyone says her name. I don't know what is happening at home. Today I told our crèche head what I've seen, and she is calling his mother in for a gentle chat.

qa.q: What time does Ujjwal's mother come?
qa.a: She comes at five.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal be feeling when he stops a step away from his mother?
qa.a: He may feel drawn to her and afraid at once, perhaps because she seems frightened herself.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Nirmala told the crèche head the same day instead of guessing alone, so someone can reach out to his mother gently.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's mother feel when she is called in for a gentle chat?
qa.a: She may feel nervous at first, but also relieved that someone has noticed she is struggling.

grounding: A crèche helper sees a toddler approach his mother then freeze or turn away while she looks frightened herself, and passes the concern on that day.

passage:
"Mumma, sit. SIT. I'll make your tea." Nandini put her hands on her hips.
"Nandini, you can't use the stove."
"Then I'll get the biscuits. You lie down. Don't cry today, okay?"
Shalini swallowed. "Beta, you don't have to look after me."
"Yes I do. Yesterday you cried and slept all day."
Nani came in from the balcony. "Nandini, come. Biscuits are my job. Your job is to play."
"But who will watch Mumma?"
"I will. I'm staying all this week, every day. And Mumma is seeing her doctor on Friday."
Nandini hesitated. "Every day?"
"Every day. You can check each morning."
Nandini climbed into Nani's lap.

qa.q: Who says she will be there every day this week?
qa.a: Nani says she is staying all week, every day.

qa.q: What might Nandini be worried about when she tells Mumma, "Don't cry today"?
qa.a: She may be worried that her mother will cry and sleep all day again, so she tries to take charge.

qa.q: What choice did Nani make, and why does it help Nandini?
qa.a: Nani took over the grown-up jobs and promised to be there every day, giving Nandini a steady adult so she can be a child again.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when her five-year-old tries to look after her?
qa.a: She may feel touched but also sad and worried, since she doesn't want her daughter carrying her.

grounding: A five-year-old bossily takes care of her struggling mother, and her grandmother steps in as a steady, consistent adult.

passage:
Class note, UKG-B, by Sharmila.
Payal, five, spent the morning managing everyone. "Ma'am, sit here. No, not there. Give me the chalk." At story time she clung to my sari, then hit my arm and ran to the corner. Ten minutes later she was back, stroking my hand. Her mother told me things at home have been very up and down lately.
What I did: kept my voice the same each time, kept the routine exactly as the chart shows, and said "I'm still here" after the hitting.
This afternoon I spoke to our school counsellor; we meet Payal's mother on Monday.

qa.q: What did Payal ask for at the start of the morning?
qa.a: She asked for the chalk.

qa.q: What might Payal be feeling when she clings, then hits, then strokes Sharmila's hand?
qa.a: She seems to need Sharmila badly but also feel unsafe about it, so she swings between holding on and pushing away.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's choices helps Payal most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the same calm voice and routine, and saying "I'm still here" after the hitting, shows Payal an adult who stays predictable.

qa.q: How might Payal's mother feel at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: She may feel anxious, but also supported, since the school is working with her rather than blaming Payal.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who bosses adults and swings between clinging and hitting, and responds with calm consistency and help from the counsellor.

subtype: Steady adult for a frightened child [Response]
passage: At the children's home in Darjeeling, Chandrika rang the little brass bell at seven every morning, the same three rings. For the first weeks, Dolma, five, hid under the bunk whenever voices rose, even happy ones. Chandrika never pulled her out. She sat on the floor and said, "Breakfast is paratha today. I'll save yours." One day Chandrika snapped at a boy for spilling milk, and Dolma froze. Later Chandrika knelt beside her. "I was too loud. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry." By the fourth month, Dolma was waiting at the door at seven, holding the bell out for her.

qa.q: How many times did Chandrika ring the bell each morning?
qa.a: She rang it three times, the same three rings each morning.

qa.q: Why might Dolma hide under the bunk when voices rose?
qa.a: Raised voices seemed to feel dangerous to her, even happy ones, so she hid to feel safe.

qa.q: What did Chandrika do after snapping at the boy, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She knelt by Dolma, admitted she was too loud and said sorry, which repaired the moment and showed an adult can mend a mistake.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika had pulled Dolma out from under the bunk?
qa.a: Dolma would likely feel more frightened and learn that adults force things, which would slow her trust.

grounding: A carer at a children's home offers the same routine, a calm tone and repair after a sharp moment, and over months a frightened child comes to trust her.

subtype: Steady adult for a frightened child [Response]
passage: Our neighbour Francis started fostering Ira last spring. She was five and flinched at everything, even his laugh. I've watched them from my balcony for months. Every evening at six he waters the tulsi pot, and she sits on the step with her doll. Same time, same step. Once she threw her plate, and he didn't shout. He said, "Plates break. You're safe. Let's sweep together." Some days she still backs away from him. But last week I saw her take his hand to cross the lane without checking his face first. I don't know what's in her head. It just looked like trust.

qa.q: What does Francis water every evening at six?
qa.a: He waters the tulsi pot.

qa.q: What might Ira be feeling when she takes Francis's hand without checking his face first?
qa.a: She seems to feel safe enough with him now, trusting him without watching for danger.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make when Ira threw her plate, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stayed calm, told her she was safe and invited her to sweep together, which showed her an adult who does not explode.

qa.q: How might Francis feel on the days Ira still backs away?
qa.a: He may feel sad, but he keeps the routine steady, as if he knows trust takes months.

grounding: A neighbour watches a foster father's predictable routine and calm response to an outburst slowly help a frightened five-year-old trust him.

passage: The power went out halfway through the Saturday art class at the community hall, and the fans stopped. Suraj, ten, had been laughing with Jagdish sir all morning, showing off his painted kite. In the sudden dark and heat, a boy knocked a water jar over the kite. Suraj exploded, flinging his brushes and shouting. Two parents at the door muttered, "Send him home. Punish him." Jagdish sir didn't. He opened the windows for light and crouched, keeping a little distance. "That kite mattered. I'm not angry. I'm staying right here." Suraj went silent and stiff, staring at the floor. Jagdish sir stayed. After a while Suraj muttered, "Can I start again?" Sir handed him fresh paper.

qa.q: What ruined Suraj's kite painting?
qa.a: A boy knocked a water jar over the kite.

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling when he goes silent and stiff?
qa.a: He may feel scared and ashamed after exploding, unsure whether he is about to be punished or pushed away.

qa.q: Which choice of Jagdish sir's helped more than punishment would have, and why?
qa.a: He stayed calm, said the kite mattered and that he was staying, which gave Suraj a safe way back.

qa.q: Why might the parents react differently from Jagdish sir?
qa.a: They saw only the outburst and wanted a punishment, while Jagdish sir seemed to see the fear under it.

grounding: In a hot, dark hall, a ten-year-old swings from friendly to explosive to shut down, and a teacher's calm presence works better than punishment.

passage: In the Hyderabad tuition room above the chemist's shop, Naveen, eleven, was cheerful all hour, cracking jokes with Indu ma'am about her wobbly chair. Then she handed back his test with red marks and said, "Let's look at these together." His face shut like a door. He pushed the paper away, pulled his hood up and said nothing at all. Indu ma'am didn't scold. She put the paper aside. "We'll look at it when you're ready. Your joke about the chair was good." He didn't answer. The next week he came early, sat a little closer, still watching her face, and said, "Is the chair still wobbly?"

qa.q: What was Naveen joking about with Indu ma'am?
qa.a: He was joking about her wobbly chair.

qa.q: What might Naveen have been afraid of when the test came back with red marks?
qa.a: He might have feared being shamed or rejected, so he shut down to protect himself.

qa.q: What did Indu ma'am choose instead of scolding, and why did it help?
qa.a: She set the paper aside, said they would look when he was ready and praised his joke, which kept the relationship safe.

qa.q: How might Indu ma'am feel when Naveen comes early the next week?
qa.a: She may feel hopeful, seeing that her calm response made him willing to return and sit closer.

grounding: A boy shifts from friendly to shut down when corrected, and a tutor's calm, non-punishing response lets him slowly come back.

passage: Payal waited outside the school counsellor's room, reading Kunal's last message again: "Did I do something?" Two weeks ago they'd spent every free period together, planning the science fair. Then, the night he said, "You're my closest friend," she blocked him. She didn't know why, only that her chest had gone tight and she'd wanted to run. It had happened before, with a girl in class eight. Inside, Mrs Rao listened without interrupting. "Wanting people near and then needing to escape is exhausting," she said. "We can work on this together, weekly. With your parents' okay, I'd also like you to meet our visiting psychologist." Payal nodded, then unblocked Kunal and typed, "Not you. Me. I'll explain soon."

qa.q: What did Kunal's last message say?
qa.a: It said, "Did I do something?"

qa.q: What did Payal feel the night Kunal called her his closest friend?
qa.a: Her chest went tight and she wanted to run, a fear that came just as the friendship got close.

qa.q: What turning point happened in the counsellor's room?
qa.a: Mrs Rao offered weekly sessions and a visiting psychologist, Payal agreed, and then unblocked Kunal to tell him it wasn't his fault.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt after being suddenly blocked?
qa.a: He was likely confused and hurt, wondering what he had done wrong.

grounding: A teenager who cut off a close friend just as they grew closer starts regular help from a school counsellor and a psychologist.

passage:
Ojas,
I owe you more than the three words I sent last month ("Leave me alone").
You were the best friend I'd had in years. We talked every night. Then you invited me to your cousin's wedding, to meet your whole family, and something in me panicked. I picked a stupid fight about cricket and walked out. I've done this before. Get really close, then burn it down before anyone can leave me first.
My khala noticed I'd stopped coming out of my room and took me to see a counsellor. I go every Tuesday now. It's slow, but I'm starting to understand the pattern.
I'm not asking you to forget it. I'm saying sorry, and that it was never about you.
Farhan

qa.q: Where had Ojas invited Farhan?
qa.a: Ojas invited Farhan to a cousin's wedding, to meet the whole family.

qa.q: What was Farhan afraid of when the friendship got very close?
qa.a: Farhan was afraid of being left, so ending things first felt safer.

qa.q: What turning point is helping Farhan change?
qa.a: Farhan's khala noticed and took Farhan to a counsellor, and the weekly sessions are helping Farhan understand the pattern.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading that it was never about Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas may feel relieved to know the fight wasn't caused by anything Ojas did, though still hurt by it.

grounding: A teenager writes to a friend about craving closeness, then wrecking it, and about starting weekly sessions with a counsellor.

passage: On the local bus to the high school in Sangli, Kalyani noticed the pattern. Last week Vandana had saved her the window seat every day, shared her chikki and chatted non-stop. This week she sat at the back and looked away when Kalyani waved. On Thursday, when Kalyani asked what was wrong, Vandana snapped, "Why do you care?" Kalyani's face stung. At home she almost decided to ignore Vandana for good. Then she remembered how Vandana had gone cold before, right after she said her parents had started fighting at night. Maybe it wasn't about Kalyani at all. On Friday she said, "I'm not okay with being snapped at. But I'm still your friend. Have you told Shinde ma'am about home?" Vandana stared at the fields for a long time. Then she nodded once.

qa.q: What did Vandana share with Kalyani last week?
qa.a: She shared her chikki.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel when Vandana snapped "Why do you care?"
qa.a: She felt hurt; her face stung and she almost decided to ignore Vandana for good.

qa.q: What choice did Kalyani make on Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She set a clear limit about being snapped at, stayed a friend and suggested Vandana talk to Shinde ma'am, a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt hearing Kalyani say she was still her friend?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and relieved, and perhaps safer to think about asking an adult for help.

grounding: A teenager sees a friend turn warm then cold, reads it as fear rather than insult, sets a boundary and nudges her toward a trusted adult.

passage: In the Prague school cafeteria on Monday, Oskar sat laughing with Vera, sketching silly portraits of teachers on napkins. By Wednesday he wouldn't answer her messages, and when she sat beside him in chemistry he moved seats. It had happened three times this term. Her first thought was, what did I do? Then she remembered the weeks after his grandmother died, and how he pulled away just when people tried to get close. On Friday she slipped him a note: "I miss you. I won't chase you. But tell me when you need space instead of vanishing. And please talk to someone you trust, maybe Mr Novak or your aunt." Oskar read it twice and put it in his pocket.

qa.q: What did Oskar sketch on napkins?
qa.a: He sketched silly portraits of teachers.

qa.q: What was Vera's first worry when Oskar moved seats?
qa.a: She worried that she had done something wrong.

qa.q: Which parts of Vera's note were wise, and why?
qa.a: She said she missed him, asked him to name his need for space instead of vanishing, and urged him to talk to a trusted adult, which is kind but clear.

qa.q: How might Oskar feel reading the note twice?
qa.a: He may feel cared for without being pressured, which could make it easier for him to reach out.

grounding: A teenager notices a friend who is warm one week and cold the next, sees fear rather than insult, sets a boundary and points him to a trusted adult.

passage: I'm Nazia. Looking back at last year, I can see how chaotic things were with Tanvir. When he held my hand at the college fest, I felt warm for about a minute, then my throat closed and I snatched my hand back and said something cruel about his shirt. Two days later I missed him so badly I rang him at midnight, crying. Then I got angry that he picked up. It made no sense, even to me. What's helping now: a friendship with Sheetal from my hostel that stays boring and steady, same lunch table every day, and my Tuesday sessions with the campus counsellor. Tanvir and I are just friends for now. Somehow that feels safer, and I don't hate it.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir hold Nazia's hand?
qa.a: He held Nazia's hand at the college fest.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when Tanvir held hands at the fest, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nazia felt warm for a moment and then afraid; Nazia's throat closed, the hand was snatched back, and a cruel remark followed.

qa.q: What is helping Nazia change the pattern?
qa.a: A steady friendship with Sheetal and Tuesday sessions with the campus counsellor give Nazia calm, reliable connections to practise with.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt when he answered the midnight call and Nazia got angry?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and hurt, since he picked up to help and was blamed for it.

grounding: A young adult describes longing for love yet feeling danger when it comes close, and how steady friendship and a counsellor are helping.

passage:
Mentor's note, Anirban, first-year engineering hostel.
Divyansh, 19, came to our fortnightly chat looking wrecked. He had started seeing someone, and within a week he'd gone from texting her all night to telling her never to contact him again. Then he wrote her a long apology at three in the morning. "I want someone so badly," he said, "and then it feels like danger." He talked about his childhood home being loud and frightening at times, and about missing his late Dadi, the one calm person there. I didn't try to fix it. I asked if he'd see the campus counsellor; he agreed, and we booked it together. I also asked him to join the Sunday cricket group. Same faces every week.

qa.q: Which group did Anirban ask Divyansh to join?
qa.a: The Sunday cricket group, with the same faces every week.

qa.q: What does Divyansh mean when he says closeness "feels like danger"?
qa.a: He longs to be close but feels afraid when it comes near, perhaps because home was loud and frightening at times.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make instead of trying to fix things?
qa.a: Anirban listened, then helped him book the campus counsellor together and suggested a steady weekly group.

qa.q: How might the person Divyansh was seeing have felt during that week?
qa.a: She was likely confused and unsettled, being texted all night, then told never to call, then sent an apology.

grounding: A mentor notes a young man whose longing and fear make love chaotic, and links him with a counsellor and a steady group.

passage: In their small house behind the Kota bus depot, Himani had learned to read Vikas's footsteps. Some evenings he came home with jalebis and sat close, telling her she was his whole world. Other times he barely spoke for days, and she tiptoed round the kitchen, afraid any word would push him further away. Last month she caught herself rehearsing a simple "How was work?" three times before saying it. That frightened her more than his silences. So she went back to her Saturday embroidery class with her cousin. She told Vikas, "I love you. But I can't keep guessing which you will walk in. I'd like us to see a counsellor, and I'm keeping my Saturdays either way." He didn't answer that night. On Saturday she went anyway.

qa.q: What did Vikas sometimes bring home?
qa.a: He sometimes came home with jalebis.

qa.q: What frightened Himani most last month, and why?
qa.a: She caught herself rehearsing a simple question three times, and it frightened her because it showed how carefully she had been tiptoeing around him.

qa.q: What turning point did Himani choose?
qa.a: She went back to her embroidery class and told Vikas she loved him, wanted them to see a counsellor and would keep her Saturdays, looking after herself instead of trying to fix him.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel hearing Himani's calm limit?
qa.a: He may feel unsettled or defensive at first, which may be why he doesn't answer, but her steadiness gives him something consistent.

grounding: A young wife confused by her husband's warmth and sudden distance protects her own wellbeing, stays steady and suggests professional help.

passage: In their Berlin flat, Fatima found Olga's sticky note on the fridge: "Best weekend ever. Love you endlessly." Two days later Olga moved her things to the sofa and wouldn't meet her eyes. It had happened four times since spring. Fatima kept apologising for things she hadn't done and checking her phone for Olga's mood. One evening, on a video call with her sister, she heard herself say, "I've shrunk." That night she told Olga calmly, "I care about you. I can't fix this for you, and I'm going to stop trying. I think a therapist could help you, and I've booked one for myself too." Olga cried, then went quiet. In the morning Fatima went for her usual run.

qa.q: What did Olga's sticky note say?
qa.a: It said, "Best weekend ever. Love you endlessly."

qa.q: What does Fatima mean when she says "I've shrunk"?
qa.a: She feels she has lost herself, always apologising and checking Olga's mood out of confusion and fear.

qa.q: What choice did Fatima make that evening, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She calmly stopped trying to fix Olga, suggested a therapist for Olga and booked one for herself, protecting her own wellbeing.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Fatima says she will stop trying to fix things?
qa.a: Olga may feel upset and scared, which may be why she cries and goes quiet, yet she also hears a steady, caring message.

grounding: A woman confused by her partner's sudden affection and distance stops walking on eggshells, protects herself and encourages professional support.
